messages.backup.bucket: At your storage provider create a bucket and an access key limited to that bucket; note the S3 endpoint address.
messages.backup.check: List the copies (check from time to time that new ones appear):
messages.backup.enable: Turn the timer on and make the first copy right away:
messages.backup.env: Write these lines into it with your values (S3-ENDPOINT is the address from your provider, for example s3.example.com):
messages.backup.init: Create the repository in the bucket once:
messages.backup.install: Install restic and create a settings file only root can read:
messages.backup.password: RESTIC_PASSWORD encrypts the copies. Keep it outside the server too, for example in a password manager: without it no copy can be restored.
messages.backup.restore: Restore the latest copy (the server is stopped meanwhile; on a new server install vibechat-server first and use the same settings file):
messages.backup.service: Create the backup service (it also drops old copies, keeping 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly):
messages.backup.title: Backups to S3
messages.backup.what: All data of the server lives in {dir}: projects, chats, settings, the host token hash and the saved Cursor key. Back up this folder.
messages.backup.where: Run the commands as root on the server (inside its container if vibechat-server runs in one). The example uses restic: it encrypts the copies, stores only what changed and works with any S3-compatible storage.
messages.lead: Signing in to the server yourself and keeping its data safe.
messages.ssh.appKey: The app's own key (Server card) only carries this app's connection: it has no shell and cannot be used to sign in.
messages.ssh.console: Key lost or no SSH access: open the server's web console (VNC or serial console) in your hosting provider's control panel, sign in there as root with the root password (no password set: use the panel's password reset or rescue mode) and add your public key again:
messages.ssh.login: Sign in from a terminal (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS and Linux); ssh finds a key in the usual place by itself:
messages.ssh.newUnix: No key yet and password login still works: make a key and send its public half to the server (macOS, Linux):
messages.ssh.newWindows: The same in PowerShell on Windows (there is no ssh-copy-id there):
messages.ssh.other: A key somewhere else: add -i with the path to the private key, for example ssh -i path/to/key root@SERVER.
messages.ssh.paths: The private key usually lives here: Windows {windows}, macOS and Linux {unix} (older keys: id_rsa in the same folder). The .pub file next to it is the public half.
messages.ssh.title: Sign in to the server with your SSH key
messages.ssh.why: When root password login is turned off on the server, root signs in over SSH only with a key whose public half is in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys: use the key you added when the server was created.
